cases.title: Churn Prediction
cases.business_context: You are the data scientist on the retention team of a B2B SaaS company with 40k accounts and roughly 6% monthly churn. Growth is slowing, and leadership wants a model that flags at-risk accounts each week so the customer success team (about 200 outreach touches/week of capacity) can intervene before renewal.
cases.core_question: Design an end-to-end churn prediction system: define the problem, pick data and metrics, build and evaluate the model, and ship it.

probes.question: How would you define churn as a modeling label? What prediction window would you pick, and why?
probes.why: Label definition is the highest-leverage decision in the whole project; tests problem framing.
probes.strong: Tie the window to the CSM action cycle (e.g. predict churn in the next 30 days so outreach can land in time); distinguish voluntary vs involuntary churn; fix the cohort and the as-of date so features cannot peek at the future.

probes.question: Which metric would you optimize and report to leadership? Why not accuracy?
probes.why: Checks metrics choice under class imbalance and real business cost.
probes.strong: AUC-PR or lift / recall at the CSM capacity (top-200 accounts); translate the metric into retained revenue; explain that accuracy is meaningless at a 6% base rate.

probes.question: What data would you pull, and what baseline would you beat before touching ML?
probes.strong: Usage telemetry, billing events, support tickets, firmographics; baseline = a recency heuristic (no login in 14 days) or plain logistic regression, to prove the ML adds lift.

probes.question: Churners are 6% of rows. How do you handle the imbalance, and how do you avoid target leakage?
probes.strong: Class weights or threshold tuning rather than naive SMOTE; a strict as-of feature cutoff; a leakage audit checking every feature was knowable at prediction time.

probes.question: Walk me through offline evaluation, then how you would validate with a live pilot.
probes.why: Evaluation depth: offline rigor and online causality.
probes.strong: Time-based splits (never random); backtest scored at capacity k; a randomized outreach pilot with a holdout, measuring incremental retention rather than raw model scores.

probes.question: The model is live. What do you monitor, and when do you retrain?
probes.strong: Prediction distribution drift, feature freshness, shifts in the base churn rate, intervention fatigue; retrain on a fixed cadence plus trigger-based retrains; champion/challenger setup.

rubric.check: Define the label, prediction window, cohort, as-of date, and the decision the score drives.
Pick an imbalance-aware metric tied to CSM capacity and retained revenue, not accuracy.
Name concrete data sources and a simple baseline to beat first.
Handle imbalance with weights or threshold tuning, and prevent target leakage.
Time-based splits, backtest at capacity k, and a randomized pilot measuring incremental retention.
Monitor drift, feature health, and churn-rate shifts; retrain on cadence plus triggers.

cases.title: Recommender System
cases.business_context: You are the DS for a mid-size e-commerce marketplace. Homepage recommendations drive about 25% of revenue, but the current system is just a 'most popular items' list. Leadership wants a personalized recommender.
cases.core_question: Design candidate generation and ranking for personalized homepage recommendations.

probes.question: What is the objective here? What does a 'good recommendation' mean for the business, and what would you predict?
probes.why: Framing beyond naive clicks; tests business thinking.
probes.strong: Long-term incremental revenue and retention, not raw CTR; predict purchase probability with engagement guardrails; name the clickbait trap explicitly.

probes.question: Sketch candidate generation and ranking. Why two stages instead of one model?
probes.strong: Retrieval (two-tower embeddings or collaborative filtering) narrows millions of items to hundreds; a ranker scores with rich features; the latency budget forces the split.

probes.question: What features would you use, and how do you handle brand-new users and new items?
probes.why: Feature instincts plus the cold-start problem.
probes.strong: User, item, and context features; content-based and popularity fallbacks for cold start; item embeddings for new arrivals.

probes.question: How would you evaluate offline, and why might an offline win fail online?
probes.strong: Offline NDCG / recall@k on held-out interactions plus replay evaluation; the gap: position bias and feedback loops, since the model trains on data generated by its own past recommendations; online A/B is the arbiter.

probes.question: How would you A/B test the new ranker, and what guardrails would you watch?
probes.strong: User-level randomization; primary metric revenue or conversion; guardrails on diversity, latency, returns and cancellations; watch for novelty effects.

probes.question: After launch, engagement is up but repeat purchase rate is down. What happened, and what do you do?
probes.why: Debugging a real failure mode and trade-off reasoning.
probes.strong: The engagement trap: optimizing clicks surfaced clickbait, amplified by feedback loops; add long-term objectives, diversity constraints, and exploration (bandits / epsilon-greedy).

rubric.check: Define the objective in long-term business terms, not just clicks.
Pair offline ranking metrics with online business metrics and guardrails.
Name interaction, user, item, and context data; beat the popularity baseline.
Two-stage retrieval plus ranking; handle cold start with content/popularity fallbacks.
Offline replay plus online A/B; name position bias and feedback loops.
Monitor latency, diversity, and long-term metrics; keep exploring.

cases.title: Fraud Detection
cases.business_context: You are the DS at a payments processor. Fraud is under 0.1% of transactions, a 20-person manual review team can inspect only a few thousand transactions a day, and every transaction must be scored in under 100ms.
cases.core_question: Design a real-time fraud scoring system that balances fraud loss against review capacity.

probes.question: How do you frame this as a decision problem, given the review team's limited capacity?
probes.why: Framing under a hard operational constraint.
probes.strong: Score, then route: auto-approve, manual review, or block; weigh false-positive cost (lost customer, insult rate) against false-negative cost (fraud loss); the review queue depth is the binding constraint.

probes.question: Which metrics would you track, and how would you pick the operating threshold?
probes.why: Metrics choice under extreme imbalance and asymmetric cost.
probes.strong: Precision and recall at review capacity, total fraud loss in dollars; set the threshold from a cost curve, never 0.5; report AUC-PR, not accuracy.

probes.question: True labels arrive with delay: chargebacks take weeks. How does that change training and evaluation?
probes.strong: Train on mature labels only; treat recent data as partially labeled; use review outcomes as weak labels with care; validate on time-based splits that respect the delay.

probes.question: How do you avoid target leakage and engineer features that serve in under 100ms?
probes.why: Leakage discipline plus latency-aware feature engineering.
probes.strong: Strict as-of feature cutoffs; precomputed velocity aggregates (counts/sums over windows); leakage audit for post-event fields like refund flags; lightweight model at request time.

probes.question: Fraudsters adapt to whatever you ship. How does the system stay effective over time?
probes.strong: Expect concept drift from adversaries; hybrid rules plus ML; fast retraining loop; anomaly detection for novel patterns; monitor precision by segment.

probes.question: What do you monitor in production, and what triggers an incident?
probes.strong: Score distribution, approval and block rates, realized fraud rate, review queue depth, p99 latency; alert on sudden shifts in any of them.

rubric.check: Frame as approve/review/block routing under review-capacity and cost asymmetry.
Precision/recall at capacity and fraud loss in dollars; threshold from a cost curve.
Name transaction, device, and velocity features; start from rules as baseline.
Handle delay and leakage: as-of cutoffs, mature labels, precomputed aggregates.
Time-based validation respecting label delay; segment-level precision.
Monitor score distribution, fraud rate, queue depth, and p99 latency; plan for adversarial drift.

cases.title: ETA Prediction
cases.business_context: You are the DS for a rideshare app. Riders see an ETA before booking; optimistic ETAs cause cancellations and 1-star reviews, pessimistic ones lose bookings to competitors.
cases.core_question: Design an ETA prediction system for pickup and trip durations.

probes.question: This is regression on what target exactly, and what loss? Why not just minimize MSE?
probes.why: Target and loss design with asymmetric business cost.
probes.strong: Target is pickup plus trip duration; MAE for robustness, but the business cares about underestimation tails, so consider asymmetric or quantile loss; MSE over-penalizes rare long trips.

probes.question: What data and features would you use, and what is your baseline?
probes.strong: GPS traces, road network graph, time of day, traffic and weather; baseline = historical segment averages or the routing engine's own estimate.

probes.question: Riders hate being told 5 minutes when it is 12. How do you handle uncertainty?
probes.strong: Prediction intervals via quantile regression; show ranges not points; calibrate the intervals so '8-12 min' is right 90% of the time.

probes.question: How do you evaluate, including across segments?
probes.why: Sliced evaluation, not just global averages.
probes.strong: Backtest on recent trips; slice by region, time of day, and weather; report tail metrics (p95 error); online: booking conversion and cancellation rate.

probes.question: The model must serve millions of ETAs per minute. What are the latency implications?
probes.strong: Precompute per-segment times, cache aggressively, use a lightweight model at request time, and keep a heuristic fallback for cache misses.

probes.question: A city opens a new toll road and ETAs degrade. How do you detect and fix it?
probes.strong: Segment-level error monitoring catches it; road-network changes are data drift; retrain on fresh traces and add features for network changes.

rubric.check: Define the target (pickup + trip) and the asymmetric cost of under- vs over-estimation.
MAE plus tail metrics (p95) and calibration of intervals; online conversion.
GPS traces, road network, traffic features; beat segment-average or routing-engine baseline.
Robust or quantile loss; uncertainty intervals, not just point estimates.
Backtest sliced by region/time/weather; online booking and cancellation metrics.
Precompute and cache for latency; monitor segment-level error; retrain on fresh traces.

cases.title: Ad Ranking
cases.business_context: You are the DS on an ads ranking team. Your model scores candidate ads in a real-time auction; the score feeds directly into pricing, so a miscalibrated model literally charges the wrong price.
cases.core_question: Design the ad ranking model: prediction target, bias corrections, evaluation, and monitoring.

probes.question: What do you predict, and why must the scores be calibrated, not just well-ranked?
probes.why: Calibration is the difference between ads ranking and generic ranking.
probes.strong: Predict pCTR and pCVR; the auction multiplies bid by predicted probability, so miscalibration means wrong prices; calibrate with isotonic or Platt scaling and check reliability diagrams.

probes.question: You only observe clicks on ads you chose to show. What bias does this create, and how do you correct it?
probes.strong: Selection bias: training data is censored by the current policy; position bias: top slots get more clicks; correct with IPS weighting, randomization buckets, and exploration traffic.

probes.question: Conversions can arrive days after the click. How do you train on delayed labels?
probes.why: Delayed feedback, a classic ads-ML problem.
probes.strong: Train on a mature label window; model the delay distribution to use recent data with importance weighting; never treat 'no conversion yet' as a hard negative.

probes.question: Revenue is up but user complaints about ad relevance are rising. How do you trade off?
probes.strong: Revenue vs user experience is a real trade-off; add relevance guardrails, constrain optimization, and track long-term engagement, not just short-term RPM.

probes.question: How do you evaluate a new ranker offline before risking real revenue online?
probes.strong: Counterfactual / replay evaluation with IPS; offline AUC and log-loss plus calibration checks; then a small-traffic A/B with guardrails before full rollout.

probes.question: What do you monitor after launch?
probes.why: Monitoring a model that shapes its own training data.
probes.strong: Calibration drift, RPM, auction dynamics, advertiser ROI, p99 latency; watch the feedback loop where the model's own decisions become tomorrow's training labels.

rubric.check: Predict pCTR/pCVR for auction pricing; state why calibration matters.
Ranking metrics plus calibration (log-loss, reliability) and revenue guardrails.
Impression/click/conversion logs; user, ad, and context features.
Correct selection/position bias (IPS, exploration) and delayed conversions.
Counterfactual replay offline; small-traffic A/B with guardrails online.
Monitor calibration drift, auction dynamics, latency, and the self-reinforcing feedback loop.

cases.title: Customer LTV
cases.business_context: You are the DS for a direct-to-consumer brand spending heavily on paid acquisition. Marketing needs a predicted lifetime value per customer to set CAC targets by channel, and they will bid real dollars against your numbers.
cases.core_question: Design a customer lifetime value prediction system that marketing can safely bid against.

probes.question: Define LTV precisely: horizon, what counts as value, per-user vs cohort.
probes.strong: Fix a horizon (e.g. 12-month gross profit) that matches payback decisions; distinguish cohort LTV for reporting from per-user predictions for bidding.

probes.question: Most users have under 3 months of history. How do you predict a 12-month value?
probes.why: Censoring, the core statistical challenge of LTV.
probes.strong: Treat it as censored data; BG/NBD plus gamma-gamma as a principled baseline, or ML with early-behavior signals; quantify uncertainty instead of hiding it.

probes.question: What features exist for a brand-new customer with zero purchases?
probes.strong: Acquisition channel, campaign, geography, device, landing context; channel-level priors until behavior accrues.

probes.question: Marketing wants one number per user to bid against. What could go wrong?
probes.strong: A point estimate hides uncertainty; the model will overbid on uncertain high-LTV users; use expected value with risk adjustment; once you bid on it, behavior shifts (Goodhart).

probes.question: How do you evaluate LTV predictions?
probes.strong: Calibration by cohort and by predicted decile; rank correlation; backtest on mature cohorts where truth is known; business metric: stability of the CAC/LTV ratio.

probes.question: How do you keep the model fresh as channels and behavior shift?
probes.strong: Fixed retrain cadence; monitor predicted vs realized LTV by cohort; watch for shocks like attribution changes that break channel features overnight.

rubric.check: Fix horizon, value definition, and cohort vs per-user use cases.
Calibration by decile/cohort and rank correlation; business metric CAC/LTV.
Order history, acquisition attributes; BG/NBD as baseline.
Handle censoring and cold start; expose uncertainty, not just point estimates.
Backtest on mature cohorts; calibration by decile; CAC/LTV stability.
Retrain cadence; monitor predicted vs realized by cohort; watch for attribution shocks.

cases.title: Demand Forecasting
cases.business_context: You are the DS for a grocery chain. Daily SKU-by-store demand forecasts drive overnight ordering; stockouts lose sales, overstock means perishable waste.
cases.core_question: Design the demand forecasting system from data to daily ordering decisions.

probes.question: At what granularity do you forecast, and why?
probes.why: Granularity is the key scoping decision.
probes.strong: SKU-store-day, because that is the ordering decision; reconcile up the hierarchy (store, region); balance sparsity against actionability.

probes.question: Stockouts and waste have different costs. How does that shape the model and the metric?
probes.why: Asymmetric costs change both modeling and metrics.
probes.strong: Newsvendor logic: forecast a quantile, not the mean; metric = wMAPE plus bias, never symmetric MAE alone.

probes.question: How do you handle promotions, holidays, and weather?
probes.strong: Promo calendars and holiday features; separate promo-uplift modeling; weather features for seasonal categories.

probes.question: What is your baseline, and how do you validate without leaking the future?
probes.strong: Naive seasonal baseline (same weekday last year/week); rolling-origin backtest; ensure promo and holiday features use only information known at forecast time.

probes.question: New SKUs have no history. What do you do?
probes.strong: Borrow from similar SKUs via embeddings or category-level models; hierarchical reconciliation to keep new-SKU forecasts coherent.

probes.question: Forecasts are live. What breaks, and how do you monitor it?
probes.strong: Monitor bias by category and store, stockout rate, and waste; alert on drift; retrain weekly; keep an audit trail of manual overrides.

rubric.check: Forecast at the ordering granularity (SKU-store-day) with hierarchy in mind.
wMAPE plus bias; quantile-aware metrics reflecting asymmetric stockout/waste costs.
Sales history, promo calendars, holidays, weather; naive seasonal baseline.
Event features, promo uplift, cold-start borrowing for new SKUs.
Rolling-origin backtest with no future leakage.
Monitor bias, stockouts, and waste; weekly retrain; override audit trail.

cases.title: Content Moderation
cases.business_context: You are the DS for trust and safety at a social app with massive user-generated content. A human review team enforces policy, legal takedown requests carry SLAs, and every automated removal can be appealed.
cases.core_question: Design ML-assisted content moderation that combines models with human reviewers.

probes.question: How do you combine the model with human reviewers?
probes.strong: Triage: auto-remove only at very high confidence, queue the rest by priority; reviewer capacity is the binding constraint; use reviewer labels for active learning.

probes.question: What precision/recall operating point do you pick, and why does it differ by violation type?
probes.strong: Severe harms get high recall; spam gets high precision; one global threshold is wrong; the operating point follows the cost of each error type.

probes.question: How do you prioritize the review queue?
probes.why: Ranking under harm, not just confidence.
probes.strong: Expected harm = severity x reach x confidence; factor in virality prediction and legal SLA deadlines.

probes.question: Bad actors adversarially evade the model, and content spans 50 languages. How do you cope?
probes.strong: Adversarial drift demands red-teaming and fast retrains; multilingual embeddings with extra human review for low-resource languages; never assume English-only performance transfers.

probes.question: Appeals overturn 8% of removals. How do you use that signal?
probes.strong: Appeals are free labeled data: measure overturn rate by category, feed disagreements into retraining, and audit for systematic bias in what gets appealed.

probes.question: What do you monitor, and how do you check fairness across groups?
probes.strong: Precision/recall by language and category, queue latency, overturn rate; disparity audits across groups; reviewer well-being as an operational metric.

rubric.check: Frame as triage: auto-action vs review queue under reviewer capacity and SLAs.
Per-category precision/recall operating points; overturn rate; queue latency.
Reviewer labels, appeal outcomes; keyword/regex baseline.
Multilingual models, adversarial robustness, active learning from the queue.
Per-language and per-category slices; appeal overturn as a quality signal.
Monitor precision/recall drift, queue health, overturn rate, and fairness disparities.
